questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to $(k-1)!$ for any $k\ge 4?$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the definition of factorial, we have 

$$
(k-1)!=(k-1)\cdot (k-2)\cdot (k-3)\cdot (k-4)\cdot \,⋯\,\cdot 2\cdot 1.
$$

Now, applying the factorial definition to all but the first two factors, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(k-1)! & =(k-1)\cdot (k-2)\cdot \overset{(k-3)!}{\overset{⏞}{(k-3)\cdot (k-4)\cdot \,⋯\,\cdot 2\cdot 1}} \\  & =(k-1)\cdot (k-2)\cdot (k-3)!\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $n\ge 2$ is an integer, simplify $\frac{(n-2)!(n+1)!}{(n!)^{2}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}n! & =n\cdot (n-1)\cdot (n-2)! \\ (n+1)! & =(n+1)\cdot n!\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we cancel the $(n-2)!$ and $n!$ that occur in both the numerator and the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(n-2)!(n+1)!}{(n!)^{2}} & =\frac{(n-2)!(n+1)!}{n!\cdot n!} \\  & =\frac{(n-2)!\cdot (n+1)\cdot n!}{n!\cdot n\cdot (n-1)\cdot (n-2)!} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(n-2)!}\cdot (n+1)\cdot \cancel{n!}}{\cancel{n!}\cdot n\cdot (n-1)\cdot \cancel{(n-2)!}} \\  & =\frac{n+1}{n(n-1)}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $n\ge 9$ is an integer, simplify $\frac{(n-8)!\,(n+9)!}{(n-9)!\,(n+7)!}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}(n+9)! & =(n+9)(n+8)(n+7)! \\ (n-8)! & =(n-8)(n-9)!\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we can cancel the $(n+7)!$ and $(n-9)!$ that occur in both the numerator and the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(n-8)!\,(n+9)!}{(n-9)!\,(n+7)!} & =\frac{[(n-8)\cdot (n-9)!]\cdot [(n+9)\cdot (n+8)\cdot (n+7)!]}{(n-9)!\cdot (n+7)!} \\  & =\frac{(n-8)\cdot \cancel{(n-9)!}\cdot (n+9)\cdot (n+8)\cdot \cancel{(n+7)!}}{\cancel{(n-9)!}\cdot \cancel{(n+7)!}} \\  & =(n-8)\cdot (n+8)\cdot (n+9) \\  & =(n-8)(n+8)(n+9)\end{aligned}
$$

$$
(m+2)!=(m+2)(m+1)(m)(m-1)!

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Writing a Factorial in an Equivalent Form
canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to $(k+1)!$ for any $k \geq 2?$

I. $(k+1) \cdot k \cdot (k-1)$

II. $(k+1) \cdot k \cdot (k-1)!$

III. $(k+1) \cdot k$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Using the definition of factorial, we have 

$$
(k+1)! = (k+1) \cdot k \cdot (k-1) \cdot (k-2) \cdot \: \cdots \: \cdot 2 \cdot 1.
$$

Now, applying the factorial definition to all but the first two factors, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(k+1)! & =(k+1)\cdot k\cdot \overset{(k-1)!}{\overset{⏞}{(k-1)\cdot (k-2)\cdot \,⋯\,\cdot 2\cdot 1}} \\  & =(k+1)\cdot k\cdot (k-1)!\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Simplifying a Variable Expression Containing a Quotient of Factorials
canonical_examples.problem: Given that $n \geq 2$ is an integer, simplify $\dfrac {n!} {(n - 2)!}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, notice the following:

$$
n! = n \cdot (n-1) \cdot (n-2)!
$$

Then, we cancel the $(n-2)!$ that occurs in both the numerator and the denominator:

$$
\eqalign{
\dfrac {n!} {(n - 2)!} 
&= \dfrac {n \cdot (n - 1) \cdot (n - 2)!} {(n - 2)!}\[5pt] 

&= \dfrac {n \cdot (n - 1) \cdot \cancel{(n - 2)!}} {\cancel{(n - 2)!}}\[5pt] 

&= n(n -1) \[5pt]
&= n^2 - n
	}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Simplifying a Variable Expression Containing a Quotient With Many Factorials
canonical_examples.problem: Given that $k \geq 1$ is an integer, simplify $\dfrac {k^2(k - 1)!} {k!}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we notice that 

$$
k! = k \cdot (k-1)!
$$

So, we can simplify the numerator as follows:

$$
k^2 (k-1)! = k \cdot \underbrace{k \cdot (k-1)!}_{k!} = k \cdot k!
$$

Then, we cancel the $k!$ that occurs in both the numerator and the denominator:

$$
\eqalign{
\dfrac {k^2(k - 1)!} {k!} 
&= \dfrac {k \cdot k!} {k!}\[5pt]
&= \dfrac {k \cdot \cancel{k!}} {\cancel{k!}} \[5pt]
&= \dfrac {k} {1} \[5pt]
&= k
	}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Factorials can be applied to variables, too. To manipulate a factorial expression involving a variable, we just need to remember that the variable represents a number, and the previous number can be obtained by subtracting $1$ from the variable.

So, in the same way that we have

$$
\begin{aligned}5! & =5\cdot \overset{4!}{\overset{⏞}{4\cdot 3\cdot 2\cdot 1}} \\  & =5\cdot 4!\end{aligned}
$$

we also have

$$
\begin{aligned}n! & =n\cdot \overset{(n-1)!}{\overset{⏞}{(n-1)\cdot (n-2)\cdot \,⋯\,\cdot 2\cdot 1}} \\  & =n\cdot (n-1)!\end{aligned}
$$

where $n$ denotes some positive integer.

Likewise, in the same way that we have

$$
5! = 5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3!
$$

we also have

$$
x! = x \cdot (x-1) \cdot (x-2)!
$$
